items.title: Travel agency software: the complete buyer's guide for 2027
items.seoTitle: Travel Agency Software: Buyer's Guide for 2027
items.metaDescription: Compare travel agency software in 2027: features, pricing models, demo questions and red flags for agencies, Umrah operators and B2B consolidators.
items.excerpt: What travel agency software does, which features matter for your type of agency, how pricing works, and how to run a fair evaluation and a calm migration.
body: If your agency runs on spreadsheets, a GDS terminal and a WhatsApp group, you don't have a system. You have a collection of workarounds.

That's not an insult. Almost every travel agency starts this way: a few bookings a week, one person who knows where everything is, and a spreadsheet that does the job. The problem is that workarounds don't scale. The spreadsheet gets a second version. The WhatsApp group gets a hundred unread messages. The accountant asks which booking earned which commission, and nobody can answer without an afternoon of digging.

This guide is for agency owners and managers who have reached that point and are now looking at travel agency software. It explains what the software actually does, which features matter for which kind of agency, how pricing works, how to run a fair evaluation, and how to avoid the mistakes that make a migration painful. It is written to be useful whether or not you ever talk to us.
What travel agency software actually does
"Travel agency software" is a loose term. Vendors use it for very different products, so it helps to separate three layers.

These help you search and sell travel products: flights from a GDS or an airline API, hotels from a supplier, tours, transfers and visas. They answer the question "what can I sell this customer today?"
These track leads, customer profiles, quotations, follow-ups and sales targets. They answer "who is asking, what did we offer, and did they buy?"

These handle invoices, payments, supplier payables, agent balances, expenses, payroll, reports and tax compliance. They answer "what did we earn, what do we owe, and what do we owe the tax authority?"

Most agencies start with layer 1 only, because it is what makes the first sale. They bolt on a spreadsheet for layer 2 and a separate accounting package for layer 3. That works until the three layers disagree with each other.
The real cost of disconnected tools

The cost shows up in small, boring places. A booking is ticketed in the GDS, but the invoice is typed by hand an hour later. A customer pays in two instalments, one in the bank statement and one in a WhatsApp screenshot, and neither is in the spreadsheet. A sub-agent says they paid; your records say they didn't. At month end, your accountant spends days matching bookings to payments and supplier invoices. And when the owner asks which service is actually profitable, the honest answer is "we think flights, but we're not sure."
What good travel agency software changes

A well-built travel agency management system does one structural thing: it keeps bookings, customers, money and operations in one database. A booking is entered once, the invoice is generated from it, the payment is recorded against that invoice, the supplier cost is attached to the same booking, and the profit is calculated from those numbers.

When people say "ERP" in this industry, this is what they mean. The point is not to have more screens. The point is that nobody types the same thing twice, and that every number can be traced back to a booking.

A customer messages you on WhatsApp. That conversation becomes a lead. The lead has a profile and a quotation. The accepted quotation becomes a booking. The booking creates an invoice, a supplier payable and a commission entry, and the reports show what you earned. If any step in that chain is manual, it is also a step where mistakes and delays creep in.
One database: entered once, used everywhere
Which type of agency are you, and what do you need?

The most common mistake in software buying is comparing products as if every agency had the same needs. A visa office in Dhaka, an Umrah operator in Riyadh and a B2B consolidator in Dubai all call themselves an agency, but they run very different days. Find your starting point in the table, then read the module checklist with your own row in mind.
What the software must handle well
Flight and hotel quotes, walk-in and WhatsApp customers, invoices, follow-ups
Fast fare search, quotations, invoicing, CRM, customer history
Groups, passports, visas, instalments, Makkah and Madinah hotels, transport
Pilgrim records, passport and visa tracking, group allocation, instalments, packages
Sub-agent network, markup, credit, commission, payouts
Agent portal, markup rules, credit and wallet, commission and payouts, agent statements
Itineraries, departures, group pricing, local transport and hotels
Day-by-day itinerary builder, departures, inclusions, vendor payables
Self-service booking, payment gateway, high lead volume
B2C website, online payment, supplier connections, automation

An Umrah operator needs group and passport logic, a consolidator needs an agent portal and credit control, a visa office needs document checklists and speed, and a tour operator needs itineraries and group pricing. A tool built for one can feel like a spreadsheet with extra steps for another.

Your location changes your requirements: VAT, e-invoicing and Arabic-speaking customers in the Gulf; MYR, IDR and local payment methods in Southeast Asia; BDT and bKash in Bangladesh; data protection rules in the UK and Europe. Ask every vendor how the product behaves in your country, not in a generic demo country.
The features that matter: a module-by-module checklist

This is the part to print and take into demos. For each module, here is what it should do and what to ask. Treat it as a checklist, not a feature race: a product with fewer modules that your team actually uses beats a product with fifty modules that nobody opens.

The core question is where fares come from: one or more GDS (Amadeus, Sabre, Travelport, Galileo), airline NDC or aggregator APIs. A good flight module handles fare search, booking, ticketing, PNR, reissue, refund and void in one place, and every ticket should create its invoice and accounting entry without retyping. Ask who holds the GDS contract (usually you, with the vendor connecting it) and whether agents can compare sources in a single search.
Look for your own direct contracts shown side by side with supplier rates, room-level markup and voucher generation.

Look for pilgrim registration, passport and visa tracking, group allocation, Makkah and Madinah hotels, transport, packages and instalment payments. Ask to see a real group of thirty or more pilgrims, and how a replaced passenger or a delayed visa is recorded.

For visas: country-wise requirements, document checklists and a status per applicant that anyone on the team can open. For tours: day-by-day itineraries, departures, inclusions and group pricing linked to supplier cost, so you know the margin. For transport: airport transfers, intercity trips and rentals with vehicles, drivers and route pricing.
Hajj & Umrah: how to digitize your agency before the next season

A travel CRM should hold customer profiles and travel history, run a lead pipeline, remind staff to follow up, and connect to quotations: a branded offer with a validity date that turns into a booking without retyping. Ask whether a chat lead from WhatsApp, Messenger, Instagram or your website becomes a CRM record in one click, whether you can see unanswered leads, and whether you can track targets and conversion per staff member. If your leads arrive through several chat apps, this module matters more than almost any other.
WhatsApp for travel agencies: turning chats into bookings
This is the module that separates a booking tool from an ERP. At a minimum, you need:
the books are real accounting records, not a sales log
with partial payments and a clear due amount
what you owe each airline, hotel or vendor
sales, profit, receivables, payables and cash flow

The report that matters most for a travel agency is profit per booking. Revenue tells you that you're busy; profit per booking tells you whether the busyness is paying. To get that number honestly, the system must attach the supplier cost, card charges, refunds and commissions to the same booking. A standalone accounting package can't do that on its own, because it doesn't know what a booking is.
Does every invoice link back to a booking?
Can I see the profit on a single booking, including supplier cost and commission?
Does the system handle multiple currencies, with exchange rates, in the same ledger?
Can it connect to the accounting tool my accountant already uses, such as QuickBooks or Xero?
Sales are not profit: how to read your travel agency's profit and loss

If you sell through sub-agents, look for an agent portal with markup rules, credit and wallet, commission and payouts, and online payment. The idea is one inventory, two storefronts: the same stock serves B2C customers and B2B agents, each with its own pricing. Ask how credit limits work, how commission is handled on a cancellation or refund, and whether each agent can see their own statement without calling you.
B2B travel sales: tracking agent commission from booking to payout

Your website should connect to your system, not sit beside it: online booking, enquiry forms and lead capture that land in your CRM. Check the CMS too. Can you edit pages, publish blog posts, build landing pages and set SEO tags without a developer? Does the site support right-to-left languages such as Arabic and Urdu?

Once you have more than a handful of staff or branches, you will want HR records (attendance, leave, payroll, permissions), a help desk with SLAs and conversation history, and task workflows. You don't need them on day one. What matters is that they live in the same system, so you don't add a fourth or fifth tool later.

Treat AI features like any other feature: ask to see them work on a real task. Practical uses include answering routine questions at any hour, qualifying leads, sending follow-ups, drafting trip plans and reading passports with OCR. Ask what happens when the AI doesn't know the answer, whether a person can take over, and which actions need approval. AI helps most with repetitive work, not with complex trips or a crisis.
AI trip planners: what they can and can't do for your agency

If customers reach you on WhatsApp, Messenger, Instagram and website chat, an omnichannel inbox puts them in one place, with team assignment, history and a one-click path into the CRM. Check which channels are included in which plan.
If you operate in Saudi Arabia or the UAE, e-invoicing is not optional background reading.
ZATCA is bringing businesses into Phase 2 (integration) in waves. Wave 25 covers businesses with VAT-taxable revenue above SAR 187,500, with an integration deadline of 1 February 2027.
the Ministry of Finance started its e-invoicing pilot on 1 July 2026. Businesses with revenue of AED 50 million or more must go live by 1 January 2027, and other businesses by 1 July 2027.
Which countries' e-invoicing do you support, and at what stage (for example, which ZATCA phase)?
Who keeps the system compliant when the rules change?
Can I see a sample compliant invoice?

TravelSuite ERP is adding e-invoicing for eight countries on the Business plan: Saudi Arabia (ZATCA), the UAE, Oman, Egypt, Jordan, Türkiye, Malaysia and Indonesia. Ask our team for the go-live date in your country, and always check your own requirements with the official tax authority.

Passport OCR sounds small until you process fifty applicants for one group, so ask how staff correct a wrongly read field. If you resell or want your own brand, look for white-label options (logo, colours, domain, email templates, branded PDF invoices, e-tickets and vouchers) and check whether they are included in every plan.
An ERP is only as useful as what it connects to. Check these categories:
GDS, airline NDC and aggregator APIs
card gateways, wallets and local methods, such as bKash and SSLCommerz in Bangladesh
WhatsApp, Messenger, Instagram, SMS and email
QuickBooks, Xero, Google Analytics and Google Maps

A reasonable model, and the one we use at TravelSuite, is that the agency brings its own supplier credentials and the vendor connects them. That keeps your supplier relationships and contracts yours. New integrations can usually be requested, so ask about the timeline and the cost.
Copy this into a spreadsheet and score each vendor from 0 to 3 on every line.
Flights, hotels, visa, Umrah, tours and transport that you actually sell
Lead capture, quotation to booking, follow-up
Booking-linked invoices, payables, profit per booking, multi-currency
Practical automation, chat channels in one inbox
Your suppliers, payment methods and accounting tool
How travel agency software is priced
Pricing pages look simple, but the way a vendor charges can change your true cost a lot. These are the models you will meet.

You pay a recurring fee, usually tiered by features, users and branches, and many vendors discount annual billing. Low upfront cost, updates included and predictable bills; but you keep paying, and the features you really need often sit in a higher tier.

Per-user pricing looks cheap for three staff and expensive for thirty, so ask whether sub-agents or part-timers count as users. Per-booking fees can suit very small agencies and hurt busy ones, so do the maths at your expected volume.

You pay once and the software runs on your own server: no recurring licence fee and more control over your data. Ask who installs it, who handles backups, security and upgrades, and how long updates are included.
Larger setups with custom development, mobile apps or direct integrations are quoted individually.

Ask for a written first-year total. Check what each plan includes and what is sold as an add-on, how many users and branches are covered, whether setup, branding, training and data migration are included, whether payment gateway or SMS charges are extra, whether there are caps on bookings or storage, and how you export your data if you leave.

How to evaluate vendors: a fair process, demo questions and red flags
Most agencies choose software after one or two demos and a price. A better process takes a few extra days and saves months of regret.
Step 1: Write down your five worst daily problems

Before you look at any product, write down the five things that cost you the most time or money. For example: retyping fares into invoices, not knowing who owes you what, visa status living in WhatsApp, a month end that takes a week, and chat leads that get lost. Those five problems are your test. A product that solves them is better for you than a product with a longer feature list.
Step 2: Shortlist three vendors, not ten
Compare three vendors seriously. With more than that, you will remember none of them clearly. Pick vendors who serve agencies like yours: the same type and the same region.
Step 3: Give every vendor the same script
Prepare one realistic scenario and ask each vendor to run it live. For a retail agency:

A customer asks for two tickets and a three-night hotel stay. Quote it, convert the quote to a booking, issue the invoice, take a part payment, record the supplier cost, and show me the profit on this booking.
For a Hajj and Umrah operator:
Register a group of 30 pilgrims, attach passports and visas, set an instalment plan, assign hotels in Makkah and Madinah, and show me who has an overdue payment.
Create a sub-agent, set a markup and a credit limit, let them make a booking, and show me their statement and the commission.
Watching three vendors run the same script is the most reliable comparison you can make.
Step 4: Ask these questions in every demo
Can I see this done live, not in slides? Which features are on my plan and which cost extra? What can't your product do? A confident vendor will answer that directly.
Where is my data hosted, and who can access it? How are backups handled? Can I export all my data if I leave? How do you control which staff can see passports and financial data?
How do you keep e-invoicing and tax features current, and who is responsible when a rule changes?
What are your support hours, time zone and languages? Who trains my staff, and how? What happens in the first 30 days?
What is the total cost in year one, including setup and add-ons? What is the contract length and the cancellation process?
Step 5: Talk to a real customer, then run a pilot

Ask for a reference from a similar agency in a similar market. If you can, pilot one real workflow, such as a single branch or one Umrah group, before you commit. Real data finds problems that demos never show.
No live demo of your scenario
"We can do that" with no timeline or proof
No clear owner for compliance changes, which is a deal-breaker in Saudi Arabia and the UAE
Support hours that miss your busy hours
A demo spent attacking other products
The fear of losing ten years of customer history keeps more agencies stuck than any price tag. The fear is reasonable, and it is manageable if you treat migration as a project, not an afterthought.
logo, colours, domain and email templates
the services you sell, markup and discount rules, currencies, taxes, roles and permissions
your supplier credentials connected to the system
customers, suppliers, agents and, where relevant, opening balances

With TravelSuite ERP, most agencies go live in 7 to 14 days, including branding, domain, payment gateway, data import and staff training. Your timeline depends on how much data you bring and how many modules you switch on.
Before you start: clean your data.

Remove duplicates, fix obvious errors and decide what you really need. You rarely need ten years of every record in the new system. Active customers, open balances, open bookings and supplier details come first.
Week 1: decide what to import and what to archive.
Typical imports are the customer, supplier and agent lists and the opening balances. Historical bookings can often be archived as exports instead of being imported line by line.
Weeks 1 and 2: test with a sample.
Import a sample, check names, phone numbers, balances and currencies, and fix the mapping before you import everything.
For a short period, check the key numbers in both systems. Don't leave the old tool running for months, or your team will drift back to it.
After go-live: review weekly for the first month.
Ask staff what slows them down. Small settings changes usually fix most complaints.

Switching on every module at once, skipping staff training, having no internal project owner, importing messy data, forgetting role permissions and defining no measure of success. Pick two or three numbers up front, such as the time to produce an invoice, the time to close the month and the number of unanswered leads, and check them after 30 and 90 days.

Most agencies choose a managed cloud, because backups, updates and uptime are handled for them. Some prefer to run the software on their own server, especially with a lifetime licence. The trade-off is control versus responsibility. Our pricing page compares the cloud plans and the lifetime licence side by side.

faqs: What is travel agency software?

Travel agency software helps an agency sell travel products, manage customers and run the business behind the sale: booking tools for flights, hotels, visas and tours, a CRM for leads and quotations, and back-office functions such as invoicing, supplier payables, reports and tax compliance. When all of these share one database, it is usually called a travel agency ERP or travel agency management system. Judge a product by what it does, not by its label: does a booking automatically produce an invoice, a supplier payable and a profit figure?
How much does travel agency software cost?

Prices range widely. Simple tools start at tens of dollars per month, while enterprise systems with custom development are quoted individually. The final cost depends on the plan, the number of users and branches, the modules you need, setup and training, and add-ons such as payment gateway or messaging fees. Ask every vendor for a written first-year total. TravelSuite ERP's current plans and prices are on our pricing page.
Do I need software with GDS integration?

Not every agency does. If you sell many flights and your agents already work in a GDS, you will want your system to connect to it. If you mostly sell visas, tours or Umrah packages, you may not. Check who holds the GDS contract and which plan includes the connection. With TravelSuite ERP, GDS API integration is part of the Enterprise plan.
Can travel agency software handle Hajj and Umrah groups?

Some can and some can't. Look for pilgrim registration, passport and visa tracking, group allocation, Makkah and Madinah hotels, transport, packages and instalment payments, and test it with a real group of thirty or more people before you commit. Hajj rules and quotas differ by country, so confirm anything country-specific with the official authority in your market.
Is cloud-based or self-hosted travel agency software better?

Cloud software is usually easier, because backups and updates are handled for you. Self-hosted software gives you more control but makes you responsible for the server, security and backups, unless the vendor maintains them for you. Compare both on price, support and who does the maintenance.
Can I switch from my current software without losing data?

Usually yes, with planning. Clean your data first, decide what to import and what to archive, test with a sample, and run both systems side by side for a short time. Ask any vendor exactly which data they import, in which format, and who does the work.

items.seoTitle: How to Digitize Your Hajj & Umrah Agency — TravelSuite ERP
items.excerpt: A practical plan to move pilgrim registration, packages and instalments out of spreadsheets.
body: Every season, Hajj and Umrah agencies handle hundreds of pilgrims with passports, visas, rooms, transport and instalment payments. When all of that lives in spreadsheets and notebooks, mistakes are expensive and stressful.
Put every pilgrim in one register with passport details, photo, contact and emergency contact. This single list becomes the source for visas, rooms, flights and payments.
Define each package with its flights, Makkah and Madinah hotels, transport and services. When a pilgrim joins a package, everything they need is attached automatically.
Record every instalment against the pilgrim's file
Send due reminders by SMS and WhatsApp
See total collected and outstanding per group
With the register, packages and payments connected, your team can focus on serving pilgrims instead of reconciling lists.

takeaways: Keep one pilgrim register as the single source of truth
Link packages to flights, hotels and transport
Automate instalment reminders
blocks: Group pilgrims by departure and assign rooms as soon as hotels are confirmed. Exported lists for hotels, transport companies and guides prevent last-minute confusion in Makkah and Madinah.
Track visas and documents per pilgrim
A checklist on every file shows which documents are missing and where each visa stands. Managers can filter the register to see only pilgrims with pending items.
At the end of the season, compare collections, supplier costs and expenses per package. These numbers guide pricing for the next season.
faqs: How long does it take to move an Umrah agency online?
Most agencies are running within two weeks, including importing existing pilgrim lists.
Can pilgrims pay online?
Yes. Send payment links for card, PayPal or Apple Pay, or record bank and cash payments.

items.title: B2B travel sales: tracking agent commission from booking to payout
items.seoTitle: How to Track B2B Agent Commission — TravelSuite ERP
items.metaDescription: How travel agencies can link every B2B sale to the agent, release commission only when bookings complete and pay agents from a clear available balance.
items.excerpt: Partner agents bring sales, but unclear commission costs trust. Here is how to track what every agent earns, from booking to payout.
body: Partner agents can bring a large share of a travel agency's sales, and they stay loyal when they are paid correctly and on time. When commission lives in a spreadsheet, agents are paid late, paid twice or paid on bookings that were later cancelled.
Link every sale to the agent
Select the agent on each hotel, tour, visa or Hajj & Umrah booking. The sale and its commission are then attributed to that agent, so you always know which partner brought which customer.
Use one default rule for all agents, as a percentage or a fixed amount per booking, and give individual agents their own rate where you have agreed one.
Agree the rate in writing before the first booking
Use a fixed amount for low-value services such as visas
Review special rates when an agent's volume changes

takeaways: Attribute every booking to the agent who brought it
Release commission only when the booking is completed
Pay out from the available balance, not from memory
blocks: Release commission at the right moment

Commission can become available when a booking is confirmed or when it is completed. Waiting for completion is safer: a booking cancelled before travel never reaches the agent's available balance, so you never pay commission on a sale you lost.

For every agent, keep three figures side by side: commission earned, commission already paid and the balance available now. Pay any amount up to the available balance, and both sides can see exactly what is still owed.
Grow the agents who grow you
Rank agents by bookings, sales and commission earned every month. It shows which partners deserve more attention and which ones have gone quiet.
faqs: Should commission be a percentage or a fixed amount?

Percentages suit high-value services such as packages and tours. A fixed amount is simpler for low-value, high-volume services such as visas. Many agencies use a percentage as the default and fixed rates for specific agents.
When should an agent be paid?
Pay from the available balance on an agreed schedule, such as weekly or monthly. If commission is released only when bookings are completed, cancelled sales are never paid out.
How does TravelSuite ERP handle agent commission?
Agents are selected on bookings, commission is calculated from the default or the agent's own rate, and Commissions & Payouts shows the earned, paid and available amounts for every agent.

items.title: Sales are not profit: how to read your travel agency's profit and loss
items.seoTitle: Travel Agency Profit and Loss, Explained — TravelSuite ERP
items.metaDescription: A practical guide for travel agencies: track paid and due invoices, link supplier costs to bookings, record refunds and read profit on a cash or accrual basis.
items.excerpt: Sales are not profit. Learn how invoices, supplier costs and refunds add up to what your agency really earns.
body: Travel agencies move large amounts of money that is not theirs to keep: hotel costs, supplier bills, visa fees and agent commission. Money in the bank is not profit until every one of those costs has been counted.
Start with paid and due on every invoice
Each booking should become an invoice with its items and due date. As payments are recorded against it, the invoice moves from unpaid to partial to paid, and the balance still due is always visible.

Record supplier costs as expenses with a category, such as accommodation or vendor services, and link them to the booking they belong to. The cost of a sale then sits next to its income instead of in a separate notebook.
Approve expenses before they are paid
Pay suppliers on their agreed payment terms
Watch the bills that fall due in the next seven days

takeaways: Money in the bank is not the same as profit
Link every supplier cost to the booking it belongs to
Read profit on both a cash and an accrual basis
blocks: Record refunds against the original payment
When a trip is cancelled, record the refund against the payment it reverses, with the reason and the method. Refunds then reduce net income in the right period and never disappear from the records.

On a cash basis, profit counts only money actually received and paid. On an accrual basis, it also includes invoices and approved bills that are still due. Cash shows what you can spend today; accrual shows what the business really earned in the period. Look at both.
Read the profit and loss every month

Income received, refunds, expenses paid, net profit and margin for the month show whether the agency is growing or only getting busier. Compare the top income sources and top expense categories to see where to act.
faqs: Do I still need an accountant?
Your team records invoices, payments and expenses as they happen. An accountant can then review the reports and prepare your statutory accounts and tax returns.
Which is better, cash or accrual basis?
Neither replaces the other. Use the cash basis to manage cash flow and the accrual basis to judge the real profit of a period.
Does TravelSuite ERP produce a profit and loss report?
Yes. The Profit & Loss report covers any date range on a cash or accrual basis, with print and export.

Track reply times, leads qualified after hours and time saved per itinerary. These numbers show whether AI is paying for itself.
faqs: Will AI replace travel consultants?
No. It handles repetitive drafting and questions so consultants can focus on selling and service.
Which languages does the AI support?
English, Arabic, Bangla, Malay and many others.

items.title: Checklist: choosing the right travel ERP for your agency
items.excerpt: Ten questions to ask any vendor before you move your agency to a new system.
body: Switching systems is a big decision. The right travel ERP saves time every day; the wrong one creates double work. Use this checklist when you compare options.
Does it handle every service you sell, including Hajj & Umrah?
Do bookings post to accounts automatically?
Is there a B2B portal with credit limits?
Does it support bKash, Nagad and local banks?
Can staff use it in Bangla?
Can you host it on your own server?
Ask for a demo with your own workflows, not a generic tour. It is the fastest way to see whether a system fits.

takeaways: List every service and workflow you run today
Check payments for every market you serve
Ask for a demo with your own data
blocks: Think about every market you sell to
If you sell to customers in the GCC, Malaysia or the USA, check that the system supports their currencies, languages and payment methods such as Visa, Mastercard, PayPal, Stripe and Apple Pay.
Pick a quiet period, import customers and balances first, train staff in short sessions and run old and new systems side by side for one or two weeks.
faqs: How much does a travel ERP cost?
Cloud plans usually start at a monthly fee, while self-hosted licenses are a one-time payment. See our pricing page for current plans.
Can I try before I buy?
Yes. Book a guided demo with sample data based on your workflows.
